atlas-pt.0069: BPI (12 months), Novobanco (9 months), EDP (18 months), Galp (one year), Jerónimo Martins (two years) and Sonae (Contacto, more than 80 places in 2026) all run annual programmes, mostly with applications between February and June and a September start.
atlas-pt.0070: Places are scarce: Jerónimo Martins took 11 people from more than 1,400 applications in 2025. The Big Four also run graduate programmes; KPMG Portugal added 223 recent graduates in 2024.
atlas-pt.0071: Técnico’s Jobshop (28 to 30 April 2026) calls itself the largest university job fair in Portugal; Nova SBE’s career fair on 17 September 2026 brought 43 organisations, including Bain, Accenture, KPMG, the ECB and the OECD; Católica’s RUMO in Porto in November 2025 had 67 companies.
atlas-pt.0072: Posted vacancies, including shared-service and tech centres
atlas-pt.0073: Net-Empregos, which calls itself Portugal’s largest job portal, showed 61,690 active offers on 8 October 2026, with a filter for internships (estágio).
atlas-pt.0074: Tech employers in Lisbon are mostly foreign engineering hubs, and recent lay-offs hit junior developers first; Landing.jobs, a tech job platform with an office in Lisbon, also offers visa and relocation help. This is also the usual route for the experienced hire.
atlas-pt.0076: Public bodies open competitions under the general public-employment law (LTFP) and publish the notice in the Diário da República and in full on the Bolsa de Emprego Público (BEP). A municipality’s notice of August 2026 for one civil-engineering post gave 10 working days to apply.
atlas-pt.0078: A personal recommendation still opens doors in smaller firms; international centres and the large groups rely on ads, fairs and structured programmes. No survey read measures how many hires come this way.
atlas-pt.0079: Expats rank Portugal last of 31 countries for career prospects, and unemployment among under-25s was 19.8% in August 2026 against 15.4% in the EU; in a slowdown the subsidised internship becomes the main door.
atlas-pt.0080: The programme calendar runs from February to June: BPI opened in February and March, Sonae’s Contacto closed on 6 April, and Novobanco took applications from 20 April to 14 June 2026. Most programmes start in September.
atlas-pt.0081: The state internship has its own window, from 12 October to 7 December 2026; outside programmes and internships, vacancies are posted all year.
atlas-pt.0082: Nova SBE’s master’s in management is 2nd in the FT 2026 table, with 93% international students, and Católica Lisbon is 25th (97% employed at three months); many Nova graduates work outside Portugal, so its pay figure is not Portuguese pay.
atlas-pt.0083: Employers recruit visibly at Técnico (Lisbon), Nova SBE and Católica (Porto), where Banco de Portugal, BPI, CGD, KPMG, Deloitte and PwC were among the 67 companies at RUMO.
atlas-pt.0084: Foreign degrees need no recognition for most private-sector jobs; the DGES offers automatic recognition for €32.20 if you want a certificate of the Portuguese equivalent.
atlas-pt.0085: Técnico Lisboa’s Jobshop, run by the students’ union AEIST, took place from 28 to 30 April 2026 on the Alameda campus, with workshops, roundtables and a finalist check-in.
atlas-pt.0086: The Nova SBE Career Fair of 17 September 2026 had 43 organisations from 50 markets, about 2,500 students expected and, for the first time, Citi, the ECB, the OECD and TikTok.
atlas-pt.0087: Católica’s RUMO in Porto was held on 12 and 13 November 2025 with 67 companies from banking, pharmaceuticals, IT and human resources, with CV sessions for students.
atlas-pt.0088: BPI’s 12-month Trainee Program (applications in February and March, start in September, open-ended contract) takes bachelor’s and master’s graduates in economics, management, engineering, mathematics or IT; Novobanco’s 9-month Young Talent Program accepts any field for corporate profiles.
atlas-pt.0089: Caixa Geral de Depósitos, Banco de Portugal and BPI were among the 67 companies at Católica’s RUMO in Porto in 2025.
atlas-pt.0090: The Big Four run graduate programmes for economics, management, law, engineering and technology graduates; KPMG Portugal added 223 people through its programme in 2024. KPMG, Deloitte and PwC were all at Católica’s RUMO in Porto.
atlas-pt.0091: Accenture, Arthur D. Little, Bain & Company, KPMG and Simon-Kucher took part in the Nova SBE Career Fair of September 2026, which also held Talent Breakfasts for students of the school’s international master’s in management and finance.
atlas-pt.0092: EDP’s 18-month Global Graduate Program has three rotations from September; Generation Galp is a one-year traineeship; Jerónimo Martins’ two-year Trainee Programme takes master’s graduates preferably in management, economics or finance.
atlas-pt.0093: Sonae’s Contacto, created in 1986, aimed to recruit more than 80 people in 2026 from economics, management, information technology, data analysis and artificial intelligence.
atlas-pt.0094: Central and local government hire through competitions under the LTFP, published on the BEP; the post in the notice read was permanent, required a degree in the field and professional-body membership, and was open for 10 working days.
atlas-pt.0095: Lisbon’s tech employers are mostly foreign engineering hubs, the largest being Mercedes-Benz.io with about 1,100 people, but recent lay-offs hit junior developers first and hiring now centres on senior engineers. Consultancies such as Capgemini run trainee academies for computer-engineering graduates.
atlas-pt.0096: Novobanco’s programme has a technology profile that requires a STEM background, and BPI asks for advanced digital literacy in its IT department.
atlas-pt.0097: Sonae’s Contacto lists data analysis and artificial intelligence among its target fields in 2026.
atlas-pt.0098: The big programmes recruit once a year: BPI in February and March, Sonae until early April, Novobanco from 20 April to 14 June, the state internship from 12 October to 7 December; ordinary vacancies are posted all year.
atlas-pt.0099: Galp and Jerónimo Martins ask for a master’s, while BPI and Novobanco accept a bachelor’s or a master’s degree.
atlas-pt.0100: Access to most non-regulated professions is free and depends on each employer; the DGES recognises foreign degrees as a Portuguese bachelor’s, master’s or doctorate (automatic recognition €32.20, within 30 days of a complete file; level and specific recognition at public universities, within 90 days). Regulated professions need the competent professional body.
atlas-pt.0101: Programmes and the Big Four visibly recruit at Técnico, Nova SBE and Católica fairs, but the programmes read ask for a degree and tests and name no list of schools.
atlas-pt.0102: The entry at graduate level is the professional internship (estágio) of about six months, not a dual-study degree; IEFP’s scheme is for graduates registered with the service.
atlas-pt.0103: Public bodies hire through competitions under the LTFP published on the BEP, but the graduate programmes read are all at banks, energy and retail groups and the Big Four.
atlas-pt.0104: The residence visa for subordinate work needs a work contract or a promise of one (Lei 23/2007, art. 59), so the employer has to commit before you move; EDP says Portuguese is not required, but Novobanco and BPI make it mandatory. See Visas for the rules.
atlas-pt.0105: A headshot is common but not mandatory, usually in the right-hand corner; E-Konomista calls a photo customary in Portugal, unlike in Brazil.
atlas-pt.0106: E-Konomista advises one page, two at most, with a 3 to 4 line summary; Expatica says no longer than three sides of A4. Europass is widely recognised, though its templates look dated.
atlas-pt.0107: A cover letter (carta de motivação) is not always required but may help you stand out; if sent, it is typed, one page, and addressed to a named HR person where possible.
atlas-pt.0108: References are not required in the application; Expatica suggests writing that they are available on request.
atlas-pt.0109: Programmes ask for an online application with a CV and academic information; no source read asks for certified or apostilled copies at this stage.
atlas-pt.0110: Salaries are often not advertised; they are usually discussed in the first interview, where the interviewer typically asks about your salary expectations (gross, salário bruto).
atlas-pt.0111: Labour Code art. 17 bars an employer from asking about a candidate’s private life, health or pregnancy unless strictly necessary and justified in writing; no programme page read mentions a background check.
atlas-pt.0112: Large groups and international centres hire through portals, fairs and programmes, while a personal recommendation (a cunha) still opens doors in smaller firms.
atlas-pt.0113: The programmes are applied for online, with online tests, a group exercise and interviews; Expatica notes that online or phone screening is increasingly common, though a first interview is usually face to face.
atlas-pt.0114: Portuguese is mandatory in Novobanco’s and BPI’s programmes and fluent Portuguese and English are asked by Jerónimo Martins; English is enough at EDP’s graduate programme and in many service and tech centres.
atlas-pt.0115: Novobanco’s programme has four stages: an online application, online tests of logical reasoning, behavioural profile and language, a group exercise on business challenges, and individual interviews. BPI adds presentation videos, an assessment centre and final interviews with business managers.
atlas-pt.0116: Galp’s selection runs through screening, an online assessment, group dynamics and a pitch, a business case and a final interview.
atlas-pt.0117: An ordinary job interview lasts 30 minutes to one hour, usually face to face, with HR or the department manager; some firms add several rounds or a skills test. Use the formal você unless invited otherwise.
atlas-pt.0118: Dress follows the job: a suit for senior finance, casual for a start-up. Punctuality is “a must” at work even if relaxed in private life. Candidates may face aptitude, language, personality and technical tests.
